headline: Chevron's board acts early on cost, cash and new power markets but protects its leadership model and keeps customers out of view

board.rationale: Customer outcomes appear mainly as volumes, reliability and contracted revenue: the latest results lead on production and refinery throughput [E01], and the one customer named is framed as a contract counterparty [E02]. This meets parts of the 1 anchor (customer as revenue) and parts of 3 (reliability for customers is reported), so 2. The board has not required unfiltered customer evidence in external reporting.

Directors make disclosed site visits and met frontline employees at Pascagoula in 2025 [E04], and regularly visit work locations [E03]. Visits are employee- rather than customer-facing and there is no disclosure of findings returning to the board, which fits the outside-in 3 anchor.

The most visible recent customer issue reached the company through consumer litigation over California fuel pricing [E05], with an amended complaint filed in September 2026 [E06]; the claims are contested and unresolved. There is no disclosure of an early-warning or key-customer watch list. Parts of the 1 anchor (issue surfaced via litigation) and of 3 (no evidence of escalation failure) apply, so 2.

The annual incentive weights operating and safety performance (personal and process safety, net production) at 25% with thresholds and maximums [E07]. There is no customer metric, and the 2025 operating score did not produce a reduction [E08]. A quality metric at meaningful weight without demonstrated downside fits 3.

The board approved a structural reset of the cost base, raising the target to $3-4 billion by end-2026 [E10], after a period in which relative TSR drove a 15% performance-share payout for 2023-25 [E09]. The revision followed relative underperformance rather than being clearly ahead of it, which is the 3 anchor.

The compensation committee publishes threshold, plan and maximum values [E12] and reports legacy results separately from the Hess contribution so the acquisition does not flatter the scorecard [E11]. That is transparent testing of headline metrics (part of 5), but there is no evidence of testing against frontline or external reality (3), so 4.

Committee chairs have unlimited access to management and outside advisors [E13], and the board meets the Chief Human Resources Officer twice a year on succession, with the Audit Committee meeting functional heads below the C-suite [E14]. Regular access below the C-suite is evidenced (5) but board-appointed advisers are disclosed only for evaluation and search, so 4.

The board amended its by-laws and governance documents after the Hess merger so a non-independent director could participate fully [E15], and committees review their charters periodically [E16]. The four-committee structure is otherwise unchanged; periodic review with minor change is the 3 anchor.

The company holds explicit, targeted positions on two named shifts: carbon intensity (a 2028 portfolio carbon intensity target of 71 gCO2e/MJ) [E17] and power demand from data centres, now backed by a 20-year contract [E18]. Oversight sits with the Public Policy and Sustainability Committee. A third shift is not named with targets, so 4.

On the AI-power shift the company is the first in the peer set with a long-term firm customer contract [E18]; on the 2025 price downturn it launched its cost programme early in the cycle [E19]. On Hess it moved first but closed late after arbitration. Early on two shocks, in line on the third: 4.

Board briefings regularly include outside speakers [E20] and the January 2026 appointment was sourced by an external advisor [E21]; the skills matrix covers environmental and transformation experience. Investor and customer voices are not shown entering the boardroom, so 4.

Capital follows the stated positions: the board approved the Hess acquisition for Guyana growth [E22] and the power venture has reached contract stage [E18]. Lower-carbon capital remains modest relative to upstream, so scale is consistent on oil and gas and power but not across all stated positions: 4.

The power venture moved from announcement to a 20-year contracted project within roughly 18 months [E18], and the cost programme was scaled up and delivered six months early [E34]. Delegation is disclosed only in general terms, so this meets parts of the outside-in 5 anchor and parts of 3: 4.

The Hess acquisition went through standard approval and a long arbitration before closing [E22]. Within about 15 months of closing, the board approved selling the acquired midstream stake with an expected $3-4 billion after-tax loss on deconsolidation [E26]. Standard diligence without public evidence of alternatives or a decline: 3.

Silence-based: the 36-month Item 5.02 sweep shows board changes only from retirement policy, death and merger terms, with no resignation over disagreement [E41]. Capped at 3, Low confidence, under Rule 5.

In 2025 capital expenditure of $17.3 billion ran below depreciation of $20.1 billion [E23] while $27.1 billion went to shareholders [E24]. The Hess acquisition was a large growth move, so this meets parts of the 1 anchor (capex below depreciation, returns dominant) and parts of 3: 2. Relative to peers, ExxonMobil reinvests above depreciation.

The independent directors waived the CEO retirement age in 2023 [E27], and average director tenure is 7.2 years [E28]. Against that, a new director was added in 2026 and the September 2026 officer elections show a visible executive pipeline [E29]. Parts of 1 (limit waived) and parts of 5 (visible pipeline) net to 3.

Evaluations are internal but individual director reviews are compiled by outside counsel [E30]. The board engages holders of over 40% of shares [E32], and shareholders hold proxy access and special-meeting rights; the independent-chair proposal drew about 15% [E31]. Openly accountable to owners (5) with evaluation short of externally facilitated: 4.

When prices fell in 2025 the first visible lever was cost: a workforce-linked restructuring with severance settled by end-2026 [E33] and a raised structural-cost target [E10]. Growth projects and the power venture were kept, so cost actions ran alongside reinvestment: 3.

Free cash flow excluding working capital is one of two financial measures in the annual incentive [E35], and 2025 free cash flow of $16.6 billion exceeded net income of $12.3 billion [E36]. Cash is central to incentives and messaging but carries a minority weight: 4.

The company holds AA-/Aa2 ratings [E40]; the net debt ratio fell to 13.1% by Q2 2026 after debt assumed with Hess [E38], and S&P describes a conservative financial policy [E37]. Leverage is below BP and close to ExxonMobil: 4.

Portfolio moves ran under a stated $10-15 billion asset-sale target, with about $9 billion realised by January 2026 [E39], and the cost programme launched before any rating or liquidity pressure [E19]. Proactive under a stated policy, with the latest divestment crystallising a loss: 4.

assessment_text.1: Customer outcomes are largely invisible at board level. Public reporting leads on production, throughput and returns [E01]; the one customer named is a contract counterparty [E02]. Directors visit sites and meet employees [E04] but no customer-facing programme is disclosed. The most visible customer issue surfaced through consumer litigation over California fuel pricing [E05]. Incentives carry a 25% operating and safety weight but no customer metric [E07]. This is the weakest dimension and the one where the board's attention most clearly sits elsewhere.
assessment_text.2: The board tests its metrics more transparently than most. The compensation committee publishes thresholds and separates legacy results from the Hess contribution [E11], and committee chairs have unlimited access to management and advisers [E13]. The main assumption revision, a structural cost reset, followed a period of weak relative returns [E09] [E10]. Committee structures are reviewed periodically but little has been retired [E16].
assessment_text.3: Chevron holds explicit, targeted positions on carbon intensity and on power for data centres [E17] [E18], and has put capital behind them through Hess and a contracted 2.67 GW power project [E22]. It was first in the peer set to sign a long-term firm power customer and moved early on cost in the 2025 downturn [E19]. Recent board appointments were externally sourced [E21]. Lower-carbon capital remains modest.
assessment_text.4: Reversible bets move quickly: the power venture went from announcement to contract in about 18 months and the cost programme finished six months early [E34]. Irreversible decisions get standard rigor; within about 15 months of closing Hess the board approved selling the acquired midstream stake at an expected $3-4 billion loss [E26]. There is no public evidence of dissent either way [E41].
assessment_text.5: The board protects the present more than it builds. In 2025 capex ran below depreciation while $27.1 billion went to shareholders [E23] [E24]. The 2023 waiver of the CEO retirement age [E27] and a combined chair and CEO role sit alongside a now-visible executive pipeline [E29]. Owner accountability is strong, with proxy access and engagement with holders of over 40% of shares [E32]; the first lever under 2025 price pressure was cost [E33].
assessment_text.6: Liquidity is a strength. Free cash flow is in the annual incentive [E35] and exceeded net income in 2025 [E36]. The balance sheet absorbed Hess and the net debt ratio fell to 13.1% by mid-2026 [E38], with AA-/Aa2 ratings [E40]. Asset sales ran under a stated target ahead of any stress [E39].

limitations.1: Boardroom customer discussion is not disclosed; inferred from external reporting and incentives.
limitations.2: Board pack content and advisor appointments are not public.
limitations.3: Capital allocation to lower-carbon positions is not separately disclosed at board level.
limitations.4: Delegation of authority and board deliberation on Hess are not public; 4.3 is silence-based.
limitations.5: Only one year of proxy was read in full; five-year trend in renewal relies on the 2023 announcement and board-change table.
limitations.6: Three years of audited cash flows were used rather than five.

subjects.name: Exxon Mobil (ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation)

board.rationale: Customers are mentioned as being supported during the 2026 disruption [X01], but external messaging is led by production, cost and returns [X06]. Parts of the 1 anchor (customer as revenue) and 3 (reliability of supply reported): 2. Sources: [X01], [X06]
The board and its safety committee periodically visit an operations site [X02]. There is no disclosed customer programme or evidence of findings returning: outside-in 3. Sources: [X02]

The most visible customer-facing issue reached the company through a California Attorney General consumer-protection suit over plastics-recycling claims [X03], which the company contests. No early-warning disclosure was found. Parts of 1 and 3: 2, Low confidence (single press source for the event). Sources: [X03]

The bonus pool moves with two-thirds of the change in annual earnings [X04]; safety, spills and emissions are inputs to the committee's judgement without disclosed weights [X05]. Mostly financial (1) with qualitative quality inputs (3): 2. Sources: [X04], [X05]

The board keeps a consistent strategy and states the current environment does not change it; the published outlook explicitly says the world is not on a net-zero pathway [X11]. No material self-initiated revision is visible in 36 months, but the evidence has not clearly contradicted the core assumption either: 3. Sources: [X11]
The headline structural-savings metric is defined against a 2019 base with a disclosed revision policy [X07]. Definitions are explained but not tested against external reality: 3. Sources: [X07]
New directors receive onboarding from senior leaders [X08], but no regular board access below the C-suite or board-appointed advisers is disclosed: 3. Sources: [X08]
The committee structure, including a Finance Committee, appears unchanged [X09]; no committee was retired or redesigned in the window. Capped at 3, Low. Sources: [X09]

The company publishes explicit positions with targets on named shifts: a low-carbon solutions business with stated plans [X10] and a published view on the energy-transition pathway updated in the annual plan [X11], plus 2030 emission plans. Systematic, targeted and overseen: 5. Sources: [X10], [X11]

It moved first on Permian consolidation (Pioneer, reflected in 2024 capital additions) [X14] and has run structural cost savings since 2019, ahead of peers [X24]. In line on the 2026 disruption: 4. Sources: [X14], [X24]

The 2025 appointment was sourced by a search firm to add energy-transition and capital-allocation expertise in response to shareholder interest [X12]; the skills matrix covers low-carbon technology. External voices in the boardroom are not disclosed: 4. Sources: [X12]

Capital visibly follows the stated thesis: the Pioneer acquisition (2024 additions of $109 billion) [X14] and 2026 planned investment 20% above the nearest IOC [X25]. Scale matches conviction: 5. Sources: [X14], [X25]
Delegation is disclosed in general terms (management grants awards within committee-set ceilings) [X15]; no public examples of pilots scaled or stopped within 12 months were found: 3. Sources: [X15]

The Pioneer integration delivered synergies about double the initial estimate [X16], while 2026 brought $1.1 billion of impairments [X17]. Outcomes are good but no evidence of alternatives sought or a deal declined: 3. Sources: [X16], [X17]
Silence-based: no Item 5.02 resignation over disagreement in 36 months [X18]. Capped at 3, Low. Sources: [X18]

Capital expenditure has exceeded depreciation in each of the last three years ($28.4 billion in 2025) [X13], while shareholder returns of $37.5 billion were larger still [X19]. Balanced, with capex above depreciation: 3, and the strongest reinvestment rate in the peer set. Sources: [X13], [X19]

Average non-employee director tenure is 4.6 years and nearly 70% joined since 2021 [X20], with a 2025 appointment tied to skills shareholders asked for [X12]. The age limit can be waived case by case and the CEO has served since 2017: 4. Sources: [X20], [X12]

The board introduced a retail programme that votes enrolled shares with its recommendations [X21] and secured a Texas redomiciliation with 71.3% support [X22] despite both leading proxy advisers recommending against [X23]. It did not adopt elective Texas provisions that weaken rights [X30]. Protective structures (1) with some responsiveness (3): 2. Sources: [X21], [X22], [X23], [X30]

Under pressure the company kept investment highest in the peer set [X25] with structural cost savings as the enabler [X24]: reinvestment leads, cost supports, so 4 (stops short of pricing or innovation leading). Sources: [X24], [X25]
Free cash flow is strong ($19.9 billion in H1 2026) [X26], but the bonus formula moves with earnings rather than cash, so cash metrics carry low weight in incentives: 3. Sources: [X26]
Net debt-to-capital of 11% with an AA rating [X27], and the balance sheet strengthened further in 2026 [X29]: lowest leverage in the peer set, 5. Sources: [X27], [X29]
A stated minimum cash policy [X28] and a cost programme running since 2019 [X07] preserve options ahead of stress. No refinancing under pressure in the window: 4. Sources: [X28], [X07]

subjects.summary: ExxonMobil grades C overall, with an A on external trends from explicit positions and capital at scale (Pioneer, investment 20% above the nearest IOC). It is held back by customer blindness (D) and a board that insulates itself from owners through the retail voting programme and the Texas redomiciliation.

subjects.name: BP p.l.c.

board.rationale: Customers are a reporting segment with its own metrics (convenience, retail fuels, EV charging, Castrol) [B01], and the new CEO leads the latest results on keeping energy flowing for customers [B02]. Evidence is management-curated rather than unfiltered: 3. Sources: [B01], [B02]

Directors run a structured workforce engagement programme that brings employee feedback to the board [B03], covering topics including retail safety [B04]. Findings return to the board (5) but the programme is employee- not customer-facing (3): 4. Sources: [B03], [B04]

Customer harm reached the board through a regulator: New Zealand's Commerce Commission announced fair-trading charges over fuel discounts and pricing, including a further instance after remediation [B05]. Strong direct evidence (regulator record): 1. Sources: [B05]

The annual bonus weights process safety (15%) and reliability and availability (15%) [B06], and the committee reduced the formulaic outcome by four points for fatalities [B07]. Meaningful quality metrics with demonstrated downside (5), but no customer metric: 4. Sources: [B06], [B07]

The February 2025 strategy reset revised core assumptions [B08] but followed sustained underperformance and an activist stake; the new CEO acknowledges performance has fallen short [B09]. Revision under external pressure: 3. Sources: [B08], [B09]

Targets have been redefined transparently (the cost target restated after the Castrol decision) [B10], and management acknowledges value write-offs [B09]. Occasional deep dives rather than routine testing: 3. Sources: [B10], [B09]

The board added insight sessions with leaders of the businesses most important to the strategy [B11] and holds private sessions with the ethics and compliance head [B12]. Regular access below the C-suite (5); board-appointed advisers only for search: 4. Sources: [B11], [B12]

The board redesigned its committees in August 2026, creating a nomination and governance committee and a people and remuneration committee [B13], and proposed retiring prior climate-reporting resolutions, which shareholders rejected [B14]. Active redesign (5) driven partly by turmoil: 4. Sources: [B13], [B14]

Positions on the energy transition have been reversed twice since 2020; the current reset names financial rather than structural-shift targets [B16], and transition positions remain in flux [B08]. Parts of 1 and 3: 2. Sources: [B08], [B16]

The company reset its strategy after peers had already re-weighted to oil and gas [B08], and suspended buybacks in February 2026 to repair the balance sheet [B17]. Reactive on two shocks, broadly in line on the 2026 supply disruption: 2. Sources: [B08], [B17]

The board added three non-executives in 2025 with oil and gas operating, finance and transformation experience to support the reset [B18]. Skills now cover the stated priorities; external voices in the room are not disclosed: 4. Sources: [B18]

Capital has not consistently followed stated positions: it stepped up into solar (Lightsource bp) [B36] and now intends to sell transition businesses including Archaea [B15]. Visible capital, but reversed: 2. Sources: [B36], [B15]

The new CEO restructured into Upstream and Downstream within four months [B20] and the refinery sale completed [B19]. Initiatives are being stopped quickly, though with impairments: 3 on the outside-in anchor. Sources: [B20], [B19]

The board removed its chair eight months after appointment, citing governance and conduct concerns [B21], following the CEO stepping down in December 2025 [B22]. Emergency succession following a major appointment is the 1 anchor; formal board acts are strong evidence. Sources: [B21], [B22]

The chair's removal was unanimous [B21] but was publicly disputed afterwards [B23], and two board-proposed special resolutions failed at the 2026 AGM [B14]. Decisive action (part of 3/5) with public relitigation (part of 1): 2. Sources: [B21], [B23], [B14]

The board suspended buybacks [B17] rather than use them for EPS support and directed excess cash to the balance sheet under the reset [B16]. Neither growth- nor return-dominated: 3. Sources: [B17], [B16]

The board has had three chair arrangements and three CEOs in about 18 months [B22] [B24]. Renewal is under way with search processes and new directors [B18], but it has been reactive rather than ahead of need: parts of 1 and 3, so 2. Sources: [B24], [B22], [B18]

The 2024 board review was externally facilitated [B25], but no chair review was undertaken in 2025 [B26]. After a significant vote against the chair the board committed to report back within six months [B27]: 3. Sources: [B25], [B26], [B27]

The first levers under pressure were a $20 billion disposal programme [B34] and exits from transition businesses [B15], alongside a reset of upstream investment. Mainly retrenchment with some reinvestment: 2. Sources: [B34], [B15]

Modified free cash flow carries 30% of the annual bonus [B29] and growing free cash flow is a primary reset target [B30]. Cash is central to incentives and messaging; cash conversion trails ExxonMobil: 4. Sources: [B29], [B30]

Net debt of $22.3 billion at Q2 2026 [B31] plus about $13 billion of hybrids [B33] leaves leverage above both peers; S&P rates A- with a positive outlook [B32]. Above-peer leverage that is improving: 2. Sources: [B31], [B32], [B33]

The buyback was suspended and balance-sheet repair prioritised only after sustained underperformance [B17]; the CEO says the reduction is still not enough [B28]. Action after visible stress (1), ahead of further deterioration (3): 2. Sources: [B17], [B28]

subjects.summary: BP grades D overall: customer-linked reporting and incentives and good below-C-suite access do not offset four dimensions at D, and the 2.5 average rounds down. Three chair arrangements and three CEOs in about 18 months, reversed transition positions and above-peer leverage make it the most Day 2 board in the set on decision-making and renewal.

actions.heading: Put a customer measure into the 2027 Chevron Incentive Plan

overall_summary.board: Chevron's board grades C overall (Day 2 creeping in): strong on cash, external trends and metric discipline, held back by customer blindness and a protect-the-present capital and leadership posture.

what_moved: Three dimensions pull the grade up: liquidity and capital management (B), embracing external trends (B) and resisting proxies (B), driven by an AA- balance sheet, an early contracted move into data-centre power and transparent incentive metrics. Customer obsession (D) and building over protecting (C) hold it back: customers are visible only as volumes and litigation, capex ran below depreciation in 2025, and the 2023 CEO retirement-age waiver keeps the leadership model unchanged.
headline_findings: Customers appear as volumes and contracts, and a consumer pricing suit is pending [E05].
Capex ran below depreciation in 2025 while $27.1 billion went to shareholders [E23] [E24].
An AA- balance sheet and free cash flow in incentives anchor liquidity [E40] [E35].

peer_position: Chevron and ExxonMobil grade C overall; BP grades D. Chevron trails ExxonMobil on external trends and reinvestment but leads it on owner accountability; it is ahead of BP on four of six dimensions, trailing only on customer evidence and resisting proxies.
peer_summary_lines: ExxonMobil: better on external trends (A) and balance sheet; worse on owner accountability (Texas move, retail voting programme); at par overall (C).
BP: worse on decision-making, renewal and liquidity (D); better on customer evidence and incentives; behind overall (D).

peer_row_summary.1: All three are weak. BP (C) is better: a customer segment with its own metrics and safety-linked pay with demonstrated downside. Chevron (D) and ExxonMobil (D) treat customers as volume.
peer_row_summary.2: Chevron and BP (B) lead ExxonMobil (C): Chevron on transparent metrics and access, BP on below-C-suite insight sessions and committee redesign.
peer_row_summary.3: ExxonMobil (A) leads with explicit positions and capital at scale; Chevron (B) is close, with the earliest power move; BP (D) has reversed positions.
peer_row_summary.4: Chevron and ExxonMobil (C) are at par; BP (D) is weakest after its chair was removed eight months into the role.
peer_row_summary.5: ExxonMobil and Chevron (C) at par for different reasons: ExxonMobil reinvests but insulates its board; Chevron is accountable to owners but harvests. BP (D) has reactive renewal.
peer_row_summary.6: Chevron and ExxonMobil (B) are at par with AA ratings; BP (D) carries above-peer leverage, now falling.

additional_information_needed: Board and committee agendas or minutes for the last four meetings would settle 1.1, 1.3 and 4.3, which are inferred or silence-based from public sources.
The board's capital allocation papers for 2025-26 would show whether the reinvestment rate behind 5.1 was a deliberate posture or a price-cycle outcome.

1.1.board: Customer outcomes appear mainly as volumes, reliability and contracted revenue: the latest results lead on production and refinery throughput [E01], and the one customer named is framed as a contract counterparty [E02]. This meets parts of the 1 anchor (customer as revenue) and parts of 3 (reliability for customers is reported), so 2. The board has not required unfiltered customer evidence in external reporting.

1.2.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] Directors make disclosed site visits and met frontline employees at Pascagoula in 2025 [E04], and regularly visit work locations [E03]. Visits are employee- rather than customer-facing and there is no disclosure of findings returning to the board, which fits the outside-in 3 anchor.

1.3.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The most visible recent customer issue reached the company through consumer litigation over California fuel pricing [E05], with an amended complaint filed in September 2026 [E06]; the claims are contested and unresolved. There is no disclosure of an early-warning or key-customer watch list. Parts of the 1 anchor (issue surfaced via litigation) and of 3 (no evidence of escalation failure) apply, so 2.

1.4.board: The annual incentive weights operating and safety performance (personal and process safety, net production) at 25% with thresholds and maximums [E07]. There is no customer metric, and the 2025 operating score did not produce a reduction [E08]. A quality metric at meaningful weight without demonstrated downside fits 3.

2.1.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The board approved a structural reset of the cost base, raising the target to $3-4 billion by end-2026 [E10], after a period in which relative TSR drove a 15% performance-share payout for 2023-25 [E09]. The revision followed relative underperformance rather than being clearly ahead of it, which is the 3 anchor.

2.2.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The compensation committee publishes threshold, plan and maximum values [E12] and reports legacy results separately from the Hess contribution so the acquisition does not flatter the scorecard [E11]. That is transparent testing of headline metrics (part of 5), but there is no evidence of testing against frontline or external reality (3), so 4.

2.3.board: Committee chairs have unlimited access to management and outside advisors [E13], and the board meets the Chief Human Resources Officer twice a year on succession, with the Audit Committee meeting functional heads below the C-suite [E14]. Regular access below the C-suite is evidenced (5) but board-appointed advisers are disclosed only for evaluation and search, so 4.

2.4.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The board amended its by-laws and governance documents after the Hess merger so a non-independent director could participate fully [E15], and committees review their charters periodically [E16]. The four-committee structure is otherwise unchanged; periodic review with minor change is the 3 anchor.

3.1.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The company holds explicit, targeted positions on two named shifts: carbon intensity (a 2028 portfolio carbon intensity target of 71 gCO2e/MJ) [E17] and power demand from data centres, now backed by a 20-year contract [E18]. Oversight sits with the Public Policy and Sustainability Committee. A third shift is not named with targets, so 4.

3.2.board: On the AI-power shift the company is the first in the peer set with a long-term firm customer contract [E18]; on the 2025 price downturn it launched its cost programme early in the cycle [E19]. On Hess it moved first but closed late after arbitration. Early on two shocks, in line on the third: 4.

3.3.board: Board briefings regularly include outside speakers [E20] and the January 2026 appointment was sourced by an external advisor [E21]; the skills matrix covers environmental and transformation experience. Investor and customer voices are not shown entering the boardroom, so 4.

3.4.board: Capital follows the stated positions: the board approved the Hess acquisition for Guyana growth [E22] and the power venture has reached contract stage [E18]. Lower-carbon capital remains modest relative to upstream, so scale is consistent on oil and gas and power but not across all stated positions: 4.

4.1.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The power venture moved from announcement to a 20-year contracted project within roughly 18 months [E18], and the cost programme was scaled up and delivered six months early [E34]. Delegation is disclosed only in general terms, so this meets parts of the outside-in 5 anchor and parts of 3: 4.

4.2.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The Hess acquisition went through standard approval and a long arbitration before closing [E22]. Within about 15 months of closing, the board approved selling the acquired midstream stake with an expected $3-4 billion after-tax loss on deconsolidation [E26]. Standard diligence without public evidence of alternatives or a decline: 3.

4.3.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] Silence-based: the 36-month Item 5.02 sweep shows board changes only from retirement policy, death and merger terms, with no resignation over disagreement [E41]. Capped at 3, Low confidence, under Rule 5.

5.1.board: In 2025 capital expenditure of $17.3 billion ran below depreciation of $20.1 billion [E23] while $27.1 billion went to shareholders [E24]. The Hess acquisition was a large growth move, so this meets parts of the 1 anchor (capex below depreciation, returns dominant) and parts of 3: 2. Relative to peers, ExxonMobil reinvests above depreciation.

5.2.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The independent directors waived the CEO retirement age in 2023 [E27], and average director tenure is 7.2 years [E28]. Against that, a new director was added in 2026 and the September 2026 officer elections show a visible executive pipeline [E29]. Parts of 1 (limit waived) and parts of 5 (visible pipeline) net to 3.

5.3.board: Evaluations are internal but individual director reviews are compiled by outside counsel [E30]. The board engages holders of over 40% of shares [E32], and shareholders hold proxy access and special-meeting rights; the independent-chair proposal drew about 15% [E31]. Openly accountable to owners (5) with evaluation short of externally facilitated: 4.

5.4.board: When prices fell in 2025 the first visible lever was cost: a workforce-linked restructuring with severance settled by end-2026 [E33] and a raised structural-cost target [E10]. Growth projects and the power venture were kept, so cost actions ran alongside reinvestment: 3.

6.1.board: Free cash flow excluding working capital is one of two financial measures in the annual incentive [E35], and 2025 free cash flow of $16.6 billion exceeded net income of $12.3 billion [E36]. Cash is central to incentives and messaging but carries a minority weight: 4.

6.2.board: [SIMULATED 2026-Q3] The company holds AA-/Aa2 ratings [E40]; the net debt ratio fell to 13.1% by Q2 2026 after debt assumed with Hess [E38], and S&P describes a conservative financial policy [E37]. Leverage is below BP and close to ExxonMobil: 4.

6.3.board: Portfolio moves ran under a stated $10-15 billion asset-sale target, with about $9 billion realised by January 2026 [E39], and the cost programme launched before any rating or liquidity pressure [E19]. Proactive under a stated policy, with the latest divestment crystallising a loss: 4.
